AcmeCorp Leave Policy
Owner: Human Resources
Version 4, effective 1 January 2026
Applies to: all employees
1. Purpose
This policy sets out the types of leave available to AcmeCorp employees, how much of
each an employee is entitled to, and how to request it.
2. Annual leave
Full-time employees receive 25 days of paid annual leave per calendar year, in addition
to public holidays. Part-time employees receive a pro-rata share based on their
contracted hours.
Employees who join during the year receive leave in proportion to the months remaining
in that year.
Up to 5 unused days can be carried over into the next year. Carried-over days must be
taken by 31 March, after which they are lost. Leave is not paid out in place of being
taken, except when an employee leaves the company.

Requests are made in the HR portal and approved by the line manager.
- Leave of up to 3 days needs at least 5 working days of notice.
- Leave of more than 3 days needs at least 4 weeks of notice.
- Managers should answer a request within 3 working days.
A manager may refuse a request when too many people in the team are already away, but
must offer alternative dates.
4. Sick leave
Employees receive up to 10 days of paid sick leave per year. An absence of more than 3
consecutive working days needs a note from a doctor. Employees should tell their manager
before their normal start time on the first day of absence.
5. Parental leave
The primary caregiver receives 16 weeks of paid parental leave. The secondary caregiver
receives 4 weeks of paid leave, to be taken within 6 months of the birth or adoption.
Employees should give 8 weeks of notice where possible.
6. Bereavement leave
Employees receive 5 days of paid leave on the death of a close family member, and 1 day
for other relatives.

7. Unpaid leave
Unpaid leave of up to 4 weeks can be approved by a department head. Longer periods need
approval from HR.
8. Questions
Questions about this policy go to the HR service desk at hr-help@acmecorp.example.

answers.question: What was the root cause of the last production outage?
answers.text: The outage was caused by connection‑pool exhaustion in the payments service.

sources.label: S1
sources.text:
Postmortem: Payments Outage of 18 August 2026
Owner: Engineering, Payments team
Status: Final
Audience: Engineering

1. Summary

On 18 August 2026 the payments service rejected or timed out on most requests for 47 minutes, from 10:42 to 11:29 CET. About 3,900 customer payments failed during that time. No payment was charged twice and no data was lost.

2. Impact

- 47 minutes of degraded service.
- Roughly 3,900 failed payment attempts. About 70 percent were retried successfully by customers within the hour.
- 212 support tickets.

3. Root cause

The root cause was connection pool exhaustion in the payments service.

A release at 10:31 changed the fraud scoring call from asynchronous to synchronous. Each payment request now held a database connection while it waited for the fraud scoring service. Under normal load this added about 40 ms and went unnoticed. At 10:42 the fraud scoring service slowed down, the waiting requests held their connections for several seconds each, and the pool of 50 connections ran out. New requests waited for a connection and then timed out.

sources.label: S2
sources.text:
4. Why it was not caught

- The canary stage passed, because the fraud scoring service was fast during those 15 minutes.
- There was no alert on connection pool usage, only on error rate.
- The load test in staging uses a stub for fraud scoring that always answers in 5 ms.

5. Timeline (CET)

10:31 Release reaches full rollout.
10:42 Fraud scoring latency rises. Payment error rate starts to climb.
10:46 Error rate alert pages the on-call engineer.
10:58 On-call engineer suspects the database and fails over to the replica. No improvement.
11:17 Connection pool exhaustion identified from service metrics.
11:24 Manual rollback of the 10:31 release started.
11:29 Error rate back to normal.

Owner: Engineering, Platform team

1. Scope

This runbook covers how a change reaches production for the services on the shared platform: orders, payments, catalogue and notifications. It also covers how a release is rolled back.

3. Staging: the image is deployed to the staging environment and the smoke tests run against it.

4. How rollbacks work

The pipeline rolls back automatically during the canary stage when either of these is true for 2 minutes:

- the error rate of the new version is above 2 percent, or
- the 95th percentile latency is more than 1.5 times that of the previous version.

Owner: Finance, Accounts Payable
Version 5, effective 1 April 2026
Audience: Finance
1. Purpose
This document sets out who may approve a payment to a vendor, depending on the amount.
It applies to all invoices and all payment methods.
2. Approval limits
The limit applies to the total value of the invoice, including tax.
- Up to 5,000 EUR: Finance Analyst.

A request to change a vendor's bank details is treated as suspicious until confirmed. It

A payment outside the weekly payment run needs approval one level above the normal
approver.

No vendor payments are released during the last 2 working days of the month, except
payroll-related and tax payments.

Exceptions to these limits are approved by the Chief Financial Officer in writing and
kept with the payment record.

answers.question: What is the process for a performance improvement plan?
answers.text:
**Process for a Performance Improvement Plan (PIP)**  

1. **Pre‑plan steps** – The manager must:  
   - Hold at least two documented one‑to‑one meetings with the employee, giving specific examples and a reasonable time to improve.  
   - Send a written request to the HR business partner, who verifies that these steps were taken and may refuse to open a plan if they were not. [S1]  

2. **Opening the plan** – The manager and HR business partner jointly draft the plan, which includes:  
   - The performance gaps with examples.  
   - 3–5 measurable objectives.  
   - Support to be provided (e.g., training, mentor).  
   - The plan’s length (standard 60 days; 30 days for employees in their first 6 months; 90 days for senior roles).  
   The plan is presented to the employee in a meeting with the manager and HR partner; the employee may add written comments and bring a colleague. [S2]  

3. **During the plan** –  
   - The manager and employee meet weekly; a brief note of each meeting is saved in the HR case system.  
   - The HR business partner attends a midpoint review. [S2]  

4. **Outcomes** – At the end of the plan, one of three outcomes is recorded:  
   - **Passed** – objectives met; plan closed and performance monitored for 3 months.  
   - **Extended** – clear progress but not all objectives met; one extension of up to 30 days allowed.  
   - **Not passed** – objectives not met; HR and department head decide on role change or end of employment, requiring HR Director approval and Legal review. [S3]  

5. **Confidentiality** – Only the employee, manager, department head, and HR know the employee is on a plan; the case file is restricted. Managers must not discuss the plan with colleagues. [S3]  

6. **Records** – Plan documents are kept for 3 years after closure, then deleted. [S3]

answers.question: What is the SOP for a warehouse incident?
answers.text:
**Warehouse Incident SOP (OPS‑SOP‑014, v7, 1 Jun 2026)**  

1. **Immediate actions (first person on scene)**  
   - Make the area safe, stop nearby equipment, keep people away.  
   - Call the site first‑aider (internal 555) for any injury; call public emergency services for serious injuries.  
   - Inform the shift supervisor immediately.  
   - Do not move damaged goods or equipment unless they pose a danger, so the scene can be recorded. [S1]  

2. **Supervisor actions**  
   - Confirm that Section 2 has been completed.  
   - Photograph the area, goods, and any equipment involved.  
   - Collect names of all present.  
   - Move damaged goods to the quarantine area and label them with the incident number.  
   - Determine the severity level (Section 4). [S1]  

3. **Severity levels**  
   - **Level 1:** near miss or damage < 1 000 EUR, no injury.  
   - **Level 2:** damage ≥ 1 000 EUR or injury needing first aid only.  
   - **Level 3:** injury needing medical treatment, fire, chemical spill, or damage > 25 000 EUR. [S1]  

4. **Reporting times**  
   - All levels: supervisor files an incident report in the operations system within 24 h.  
   - Level 2: site manager notified before shift end.  
   - Level 3: site manager and Head of Operations notified within 1 h by phone; area remains closed until reopened. [S1]  

5. **Forklift and equipment incidents**  
   - Any involved equipment is taken out of service, tagged, and only returned after maintenance inspection and supervisor confirmation. [S1]  

6. **Damaged customer goods**  
   - Supervisor records order numbers in the incident report; customer service is informed the same day for replacements. [S1]  

7. **Follow‑up**  
   - For Level 2 and Level 3 incidents, the site manager holds a review within 5 working days, records cause and corrective actions, and tracks actions in the operations system until closed. [S1]  

8. **Records**  
   - Incident reports are retained for 5 years. [S1]

Document number: OPS-SOP-014
Owner: Operations
Version 7, effective 1 June 2026
Audience: Operations
1. Scope
This procedure applies to every AcmeCorp warehouse. An incident is any event that
injures a person, damages goods or equipment, or could have done so. Near misses are
incidents.
2. Immediate actions
Section 2 is for the first person on the scene.
1. Make the area safe. Stop nearby equipment and keep people away.
2. If anyone is injured, call the site first aider on the internal emergency number 555.

3. Tell the shift supervisor at once.
4. Do not move damaged goods or equipment unless they are a danger, so the scene can be

answers.question: How does our deployment pipeline handle rollbacks?
answers.text: The pipeline automatically rolls back during the canary stage when either the error rate of the new version exceeds 2 percent or the 95th‑percentile latency is more than 1.5 times that of the previous version for a continuous 2‑minute period. In that case all traffic is moved back to the previous image, the release is marked failed, and the previous image remains warm for 24 hours so the switch takes under a minute. A manual rollback can also be triggered by any on‑call engineer with the command `deployctl rollback <service> --to previous`; no additional approval is required, and the reason must be recorded afterward. Deployment Runbook
Owner: Engineering, Platform team
Last reviewed: 14 September 2026
Audience: Engineering

1. Scope

This runbook covers how a change reaches production for the services on the shared platform: orders, payments, catalogue and notifications. It also covers how a release is rolled back.

2. Pipeline stages

Every merge to the main branch starts the pipeline.

1. Build: the service image is built and tagged with the commit hash.
2. Test: unit and integration tests run. A failure stops the pipeline.
3. Staging: the image is deployed to the staging environment and the smoke tests run against it.
4. Canary: the image is deployed to production for 5 percent of traffic and observed for 15 minutes.
5. Full rollout: traffic is moved to the new version in steps of 25 percent, with 5 minutes between steps.

3. Deployment windows

Production deployments run Monday to Thursday between 09:00 and 16:00 CET. There is a freeze on Fridays, at weekends and during the last 3 working days of each month, because of the finance month-end close. An emergency fix outside the window needs approval from the on-call engineering manager.

4. How rollbacks work

The pipeline rolls back automatically during the canary stage when either of these is true for 2 minutes:

- the error rate of the new version is above 2 percent, or
- the 95th percentile latency is more than 1.5 times that of the previous version.

An automatic rollback moves all traffic back to the previous image and marks the release as failed. The previous image is always kept warm for 24 hours after a release, so moving traffic back takes under a minute.

A manual rollback is started by the on-call engineer with:

deployctl rollback <service> --to previous

Any engineer on the on-call rota may start a manual rollback without further approval. The reason must be recorded in the release channel afterwards.

Schema migrations must be backward compatible with the previous application version, because a rollback does not undo a migration. A change that removes or renames a column is split over two releases: first stop using the column, then drop it in a later release.

The author opens an incident ticket, links the failed release, and does not redeploy until the cause is understood. Three failed releases of the same service in one week need a review with the platform team.

Owner: Engineering, Platform team
Last reviewed: 14 September 2026
Audience: Engineering

1. Scope

This runbook covers how a change reaches production for the services on the shared platform: orders, payments, catalogue and notifications. It also covers how a release is rolled back.

2. Pipeline stages

Every merge to the main branch starts the pipeline.

1. Build: the service image is built and tagged with the commit hash.
2. Test: unit and integration tests run. A failure stops the pipeline.
3. Staging: the image is deployed to the staging environment and the smoke tests run against it.
4. Canary: the image is deployed to production for 5 percent of traffic and observed for 15 minutes.
5. Full rollout: traffic is moved to the new version in steps of 25 percent, with 5 minutes between steps.

3. Deployment windows

Production deployments run Monday to Thursday between 09:00 and 16:00 CET. There is a freeze on Fridays, at weekends and during the last 3 working days of each month, because of the finance month-end close. An emergency fix outside the window needs approval from the on-call engineering manager.

4. How rollbacks work

The pipeline rolls back automatically during the canary stage when either of these is true for 2 minutes:

- the error rate of the new version is above 2 percent, or
- the 95th percentile latency is more than 1.5 times that of the previous version.

An automatic rollback moves all traffic back to the previous image and marks the release as failed. The previous image is always kept warm for 24 hours after a release, so moving traffic back takes under a minute.

A manual rollback is started by the on-call engineer with:

deployctl rollback <service> --to previous

Any engineer on the on-call rota may start a manual rollback without further approval. The reason must be recorded in the release channel afterwards.

Schema migrations must be backward compatible with the previous application version, because a rollback does not undo a migration. A change that removes or renames a column is split over two releases: first stop using the column, then drop it in a later release.

The author opens an incident ticket, links the failed release, and does not redeploy until the cause is understood. Three failed releases of the same service in one week need a review with the platform team.

Postmortem: Payments Outage of 18 August 2026
Owner: Engineering, Payments team
Status: Final
Audience: Engineering

1. Summary

On 18 August 2026 the payments service rejected or timed out on most requests for 47 minutes, from 10:42 to 11:29 CET. About 3,900 customer payments failed during that time. No payment was charged twice and no data was lost.

2. Impact

- 47 minutes of degraded service.
- Roughly 3,900 failed payment attempts. About 70 percent were retried successfully by customers within the hour.
- 212 support tickets.

3. Root cause

The root cause was connection pool exhaustion in the payments service.

A release at 10:31 changed the fraud scoring call from asynchronous to synchronous. Each payment request now held a database connection while it waited for the fraud scoring service. Under normal load this added about 40 ms and went unnoticed. At 10:42 the fraud scoring service slowed down, the waiting requests held their connections for several seconds each, and the pool of 50 connections ran out. New requests waited for a connection and then timed out.

sources.label: S2
sources.text:
4. Why it was not caught

- The canary stage passed, because the fraud scoring service was fast during those 15 minutes.
- There was no alert on connection pool usage, only on error rate.
- The load test in staging uses a stub for fraud scoring that always answers in 5 ms.

5. Timeline (CET)

10:31 Release reaches full rollout.
10:42 Fraud scoring latency rises. Payment error rate starts to climb.
10:46 Error rate alert pages the on-call engineer.
10:58 On-call engineer suspects the database and fails over to the replica. No improvement.
11:17 Connection pool exhaustion identified from service metrics.
11:24 Manual rollback of the 10:31 release started.
11:29 Error rate back to normal.

The rollback itself took 5 minutes. No duplicate charges occurred, because payment requests carry an idempotency key.

7. What went badly

It took 31 minutes from the page to the right diagnosis. The failover to the replica cost time and was not needed.

- Release the database connection before calling fraud scoring. Owner: Payments team. Done 20 August.

5. Outcomes
At the end there are three possible outcomes:
Passed: the objectives were met. The plan is closed and performance is watched for a further 3 months.
Extended: there was clear progress but not all objectives were met. One extension of up to 30 days is allowed.
Not passed: the objectives were not met. HR and the department head decide on a change of role or the end of employment.
A decision to end employment needs approval from the HR Director and a review by Legal.
6. Confidentiality
Who is on a plan is known only to the employee, the manager, the department head and HR. The individual case file is a restricted document. Managers must not discuss a plan with the employee's colleagues.
7. Records
Plan documents are kept for 3 years after the plan closes, then deleted.

4. The plan

Start: 10 August 2026. Length: 60 days. End: 9 October 2026.

Objectives:

1. Every shift handover report filed before the end of the shift.
2. Every incident report filed within 24 hours.
3. No more than one handover complaint in any 4-week period.
4. Complete the supervisor reporting course by 15 September.

Support: weekly meeting with the manager, and a mentor from the Rotterdam site.

5. Notes

10 August: plan presented. The employee attended with a colleague and added a written comment that staffing on the late shift had been below plan since March.

8 September: midpoint review with the HR business partner. Objectives 1 and 4 met. One late incident report on 27 August. Two handover complaints in August. HR asked Operations to confirm the staffing figures the employee raised.

22 September: Operations confirmed the late shift was one person short on 31 of 60 shifts between March and June.

6. Current assessment

Clear progress, with objective 3 not yet met. Given the staffing finding, the case handler expects to recommend an extension of 30 days and not an outcome of "not passed".
